learn.hook: A herder with no number words could still check that every cow came home: one pebble per cow!
points: Counting began with one-to-one matching: one pebble, knot or notch for each object. This leads to the natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}.
Ancient tally marks survive on bones: the Lebombo bone from southern Africa has notches, and one column of the Ishango bone from central Africa shows 11, 13, 17 and 19, the primes between 10 and 20.

In the Indus Valley, traders used standard cube-shaped weights in a doubling pattern (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...); Vedic texts gave names to large powers of 10, such as shata (100), sahasra (1000), ayuta (10,000) and parardha (10¹²).
N is not closed under subtraction: 3 − 5 is not a natural number. This need pushed people towards zero and negative numbers.
Not every system uses base 10. Counting the 12 finger joints of one hand with the thumb leads to base 12, which is why we still buy bananas by the dozen.

example.q: Using thumb-on-joints counting (12 per hand), how would you count 30 mangoes in dozens?

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers still sell eggs and bananas by the dozen, a trace of base-12 counting.

topics.title: Shunya: when nothing became a number

learn.hook: Is 'nothing' a number? Indian thinkers said yes, and maths was never the same again!
points: Zero has two jobs: a placeholder (the 0 in 105 shows there are no tens) and a number in its own right that can be added, subtracted and multiplied.
The idea of shunyata, emptiness, in Indian philosophy made it natural to think of 'nothing' as something real.
The Bakhshali manuscript, an ancient Indian text, uses a dot (bindu) to mark zero.
Brahmagupta stated rules for zero: a − a = 0, a + 0 = a, a − 0 = a and a × 0 = 0.
learn.reallife: The 0 on a lift panel for the ground floor and the 0 in your PIN code are both zeros, one as a level and one as a digit placeholder.

games.title: Placeholder or number?

The 0 in 2026
The 0 in 1.05

It shows there are no thousands
quiz.explain: The 0 holds the hundreds place empty so that 4 stays in the thousands place.

steps: As a placeholder, 0 only keeps a place empty (as in 10, 0.705, 2005).
In 12 + 0 = 12, zero is added like any number.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every zero in a numeral is a placeholder

It allowed calculations like 5 − 5 to have an answer

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Zero means nothing. Why is it so important?"
teach.praise: Excellent! Zero holds places and also acts as a real number with rules!
teach.nudge: What does zero do in a number like 105? Can you add or multiply with it?

revise.summary: Zero works as a placeholder and as a number. Indian thought on shunyata, the Bakhshali dot and Brahmagupta's rules made zero a full number.
focus: Tell placeholder zero from zero as a number.
Use Brahmagupta's rules for zero.
Know the history of zero in India.
remember: Bakhshali manuscript: a dot (bindu) for zero.
traps: Multiplying by 0 gives 0, not the number itself.

learn.hook: Brahmagupta thought of numbers as fortunes and debts. A debt of ₹50 is just −50!
points: Integers Z = {..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...} include negatives, zero and positives. On the number line negatives are to the left of 0.
Brahmagupta called positives dhana (fortune) and negatives rina (debt).
Adding: two fortunes make a bigger fortune; two debts make a bigger debt; a fortune and a debt partly cancel (subtract and keep the sign of the larger).
Multiplying or dividing: same signs give a positive answer; different signs give a negative answer.
learn.reallife: A bank passbook shows deposits as positive and withdrawals as negative; the balance is their integer sum.

quiz.q: In Brahmagupta's language, what is rina?
quiz.explain: Dhana is fortune (positive), rina is debt (negative).
steps: Answer: A debt, a negative number
quiz.mistake: Swaps the meanings of dhana and rina

quiz.explain: A debt of 15 and a fortune of 6 leave a debt of 9.

quiz.explain: Two debts add up to a bigger debt.
steps: Two debts add to a bigger debt.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts when both are negative

quiz.q: What is (−9) × 4?
quiz.explain: Different signs give a negative product.
steps: Different signs give a negative product.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger number's sign decides the product

quiz.explain: Same signs give a positive quotient.
steps: Same signs give a positive quotient.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the minus sign when dividing two negatives

quiz.explain: Numbers further left are smaller; −5 < −3.

−5 < −3, so −5 is to the left of −3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks −5 is bigger than −3 because 5 > 3

quiz.explain: Fortune 120 plus debt 200: 120 + (−200) = −80.
quiz.mistake: Adds both amounts as positives

quiz.q: How many integers lie strictly between −4 and 3?
steps: Strictly between means not counting −4 or 3.
quiz.mistake: Includes one of the end points

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I know if a product of two integers is positive or negative?"
teach.praise: Perfect! Same signs give positive, different signs give negative!
teach.nudge: What happens when both signs are the same? And when they are different?

revise.summary: Integers include negatives, zero and positives. Brahmagupta called positives dhana (fortune) and negatives rina (debt) and gave rules for adding and multiplying them.
focus: Add integers with the same and different signs.
Multiply and divide integers using sign rules.
Order integers on the number line.
remember: Same signs → positive product; different signs → negative.
traps: −5 is less than −3, not greater.
Two negatives added give a bigger negative, not a positive.
'Strictly between' excludes the end points.

learn.hook: Taking away a debt makes you richer. That one idea explains why minus a minus is plus!
points: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive: removing a debt of ₹30 leaves you ₹30 better off, so a − (−30) = a + 30.
Negative × negative is positive: −3 × (−4) means removing 3 debts of ₹4 each, which gains ₹12. The pattern −3 × 2 = −6, −3 × 1 = −3, −3 × 0 = 0, −3 × (−1) = 3 also shows it.
Temperatures, loans and profits give integer expressions: 4 °C falling by 9 °C is 4 − 9 = −5 °C.
Sign reasoning: if ab > 0 then a and b have the same sign; if ab < 0, opposite signs. A square is never negative.
Since squares are never negative, x² + y² + z² = 0 forces x = y = z = 0. With (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2(xy + yz + zx), if x + y + z = 0 and xy + yz + zx = 0, then x² + y² + z² = 0.

example.q: At 6 a.m. Leh is at −7 °C. By noon it is 12 °C warmer, then by night it drops 9 °C. What is the night temperature?

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers' profit-loss books track gains (+) and losses (−) daily; the total tells whether the week was good.

revise.summary: Subtracting a negative adds; negative times negative is positive, as patterns and debts show. Since squares are never negative, x² + y² + z² = 0 forces all to be 0.
focus: Explain the sign rules with patterns and money.
Solve temperature, depth and profit problems.
Reason about signs of products and squares.

learn.hook: Some numbers can be written as a neat fraction. Others, like √2, refuse to be caught by any fraction at all, no matter how hard you try!
points: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3 = 3/1, −0.5 = −1/2, 0 = 0/1.
Every natural number, whole number and integer is also a rational number.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q. Examples: √2, √3, √5 and π.
If n is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √n is irrational. But √16 = 4 is rational.
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more rational numbers; their average is always one of them.

example.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/3 and 1/2.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by 2 to make room: 8/24 and 12/24

learn.reallife: The diagonal of a square tile of side 1 m is √2 m long. A carpenter can measure it closely, but never as an exact fraction!

games.title: True or false?
items: Every integer is a rational number
Any integer n can be written as n/1.
π is exactly equal to 22/7
22/7 is only a handy approximation. π is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
The square root of every natural number is irrational
√9 = 3 and √25 = 5 are rational. Only non-perfect squares give irrational roots.
0 is a rational number
0 = 0/1, which is in the form p/q with q ≠ 0.
The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational
√2 + (−√2) = 0, and 0 is rational.
3√2 is irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is always irrational.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
quiz.explain: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 cannot be written as p/q. √25 = 5, 0.6 = 3/5 and −7/3 are all rational.
steps: √n is irrational if n is not a perfect square.
11 is not a perfect square, so √11 is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every number with a root sign is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is rational?
quiz.explain: √36 = 6 = 6/1, which is rational. The others cannot be written as fractions.
steps: √12 (12 not a square), π and 3 + √5 are irrational.
quiz.mistake: Sees the root sign and assumes the number must be irrational

quiz.q: Which number lies between 2/5 and 3/5?
quiz.explain: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/5 = 0.6. Their average is 1/2 = 0.5, which lies between them.
quiz.mistake: Compares only numerators or denominators instead of the whole fractions

quiz.q: Meena's calculator shows √2 = 1.414213562. Which statement is correct?
options: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
√2 is rational because the calculator shows a decimal
quiz.explain: √2 is irrational. A calculator can only show a few digits, so what you see is a rounded value.
steps: √2 is irrational: its decimals never end or repeat.
A calculator can show only a few digits.
So 1.414213562 is a rounded value, not exact.
Answer: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
quiz.mistake: Believes a calculator display is always exact

quiz.q: What kind of number is 2 + √3?
quiz.explain: A rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational. If 2 + √3 were p/q, then √3 would be p/q − 2, a fraction, which is impossible.
steps: Suppose 2 + √3 = p/q. Then √3 = p/q − 2, a fraction.
But √3 is irrational, so this is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a whole number makes the result rational

quiz.q: What is √2 × √8?
quiz.explain: √2 × √8 = √(2 × 8) = √16 = 4. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational one.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root instead of multiplying them

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1 and 2?
quiz.explain: You can always find another rational number between any two, for example 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, ... so the list never ends.
steps: Between any two rationals there is another, e.g. their average.
quiz.mistake: Counts only decimals with one decimal place (1.1 to 1.9)

quiz.q: Which of these is a rational number even though it has a root sign?
quiz.explain: √(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4, which is rational.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every square root is irrational

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: "What is the difference between a rational and an irrational number? They both look like numbers to me!"
teach.praise: So a rational number can be written as a fraction p/q, and an irrational one like √2 or π never can. Clear as a blue sky!
teach.nudge: Can every number be written as a fraction? Can you give me an example that cannot?

revise.summary: A rational number can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0; an irrational number cannot. √n is irrational when n is not a perfect square.
focus: Classify numbers as rational or irrational.
Find rational numbers between two rationals.
Know that rational + irrational is irrational.
traps: Not every number with a root sign is irrational.
A calculator display of √2 is only approximate.
Adding a whole number to an irrational does not make it rational.

learn.hook: ½, 2/4 and 50/100 look different, but they are the same slice of pizza!
points: Equivalent fractions name the same rational number: 2/3 = 4/6 = 10/15. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
Lowest form: divide by the HCF so that p and q are co-prime (no common factor except 1). 18/24 = 3/4.
Add or subtract using a common denominator; multiply tops and bottoms; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
Distributive property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c also hold for rationals and can make calculations shorter.
learn.reallife: Recipes for 4 people scaled to 6 need fraction multiplication: ¾ cup × 6/4 = 9/8 cups.

revise.summary: Equivalent fractions name the same rational number; reduce by the HCF to get lowest form. Add with common denominators, multiply across, divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
focus: Write equivalent fractions and lowest forms.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rationals.
Use the distributive property to simplify.

topics.title: Rationals on the number line and absolute value

learn.hook: How far is −3 from 0? Exactly as far as 3. Distance never goes negative!
points: To show p/q on the number line, divide each unit into q equal parts and count p parts from 0 (right for positive, left for negative). 7/4 = 1¾: go to 1, then 3 of the 4 parts.
The absolute value |a| is the distance of a from 0: |−5| = 5 and |5| = 5.
The distance between a and b on the line is |a − b|, e.g. between −2 and 3/2 it is |−2 − 3/2| = 7/2.
For a < b, the average (a + b)/2 lies between them: (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2 > 0 and b − (a + b)/2 = (b − a)/2 > 0. It is exactly halfway.

example.q: Show that (a + b)/2 is between 1/3 and 1/2, and find it.

learn.reallife: The lift display at a mall shows −2 for the second basement; how many floors to go up to floor 3 is |3 − (−2)| = 5.

For 5/3, q = 3; then count 5 parts from 0.

quiz.q: For a < b, why is (a + b)/2 always bigger than a?
options: Because (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2, which is positive
quiz.explain: b − a > 0, so half of it is also positive.
steps: a < b, so b − a > 0, and half of it is positive.
So (a + b)/2 > a, whatever the signs of a and b.

quiz.q: Which point is farther from 0: −3/2 or 5/4?
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative numbers are always closer to 0

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What does |−8| mean, and how far apart are −2 and 5?"
teach.praise: Spot on! Absolute value is distance from zero, and −2 to 5 is 7 apart!
teach.nudge: What does absolute value measure? How can you find the gap between two numbers?

revise.summary: To show p/q on the line, split each unit into q parts and count p. |a| is distance from 0, and the distance between a and b is |a − b|. The average lies exactly halfway.
focus: Mark rationals on the number line.
Find absolute values and distances.
Show the average lies between two numbers.
traps: Divide each unit by the denominator, not the numerator.
Absolute value is never negative.
Subtracting a negative means adding.

learn.hook: Between 1/2 and 3/4 there's always another fraction, and between those another... forever!
points: The rational numbers are dense: between any two rationals there are infinitely many more.
Method 1, averages: (a + b)/2 is between a and b; repeat with the new pairs.
Method 2, common denominators: write both with a bigger common denominator, e.g. 3/5 = 30/50 and 4/5 = 40/50, then 31/50, 32/50, ..., 39/50 are between them.
Method 3, extra decimal places: between 0.3 and 0.4 lie 0.31, 0.32, ..., and between 0.31 and 0.32 lie 0.311, 0.312, ...
To find exactly n rationals between two numbers, scale up the denominators until there are at least n numerators in between.

example.q: Find five rational numbers between 2/3 and 3/4.

learn.reallife: Petrol prices like ₹102.345 per litre and ₹102.346 per litre show there is always a finer value in between.

games.title: Density true or false
items: There is no rational number between 1/3 and 1/2.
5/12 is one of infinitely many.
Between 0.5 and 0.6 there are exactly 9 rational numbers.
There are infinitely many, like 0.55, 0.555, 0.5555...
The average of two rationals is rational.
(a + b)/2 is a ratio of integers if a and b are.
31/50 lies between 3/5 and 4/5.
There are infinitely many integers between 2 and 3.
There are no integers strictly between 2 and 3.

items.text: Writing 1/3 and 2/3 as 3/9 and 6/9, a rational between is ___

quiz.q: Which number lies between 3/7 and 4/7?
quiz.mistake: Thinks no fraction exists between fractions with consecutive numerators

quiz.q: How many rational numbers are there between 0.1 and 0.2?
quiz.explain: Using more decimal places you can always find more: 0.11, 0.111, 0.1111, ...
steps: Rationals are dense: more decimal places give more numbers.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one-decimal steps

quiz.q: What is the average of 1/5 and 1/3?
quiz.mistake: Adds tops and bottoms: (1 + 1)/(5 + 3)

quiz.q: To find 4 rationals between 1/2 and 3/5, which pair of equivalent forms helps directly?
quiz.explain: 25/50 and 30/50 leave 26, 27, 28, 29 over 50 in between.
steps: We need at least 4 whole numerators between the two forms.
quiz.mistake: Picks forms that leave too few numerators in between

quiz.q: Which list has three rationals between 2.4 and 2.5?
quiz.explain: Each of 2.41, 2.45 and 2.49 is greater than 2.4 and less than 2.5.
quiz.mistake: Misreads decimal places, thinking 2.04 is bigger than 2.4

quiz.q: Between 5/9 and 6/9, how many fractions with denominator 90 lie strictly between them?
quiz.explain: 5/9 = 50/90 and 6/9 = 60/90, so the numerators 51 to 59 work.
quiz.mistake: Includes one of the end points

quiz.q: Taking the average twice: the average of 0 and 1 is 1/2; the average of 0 and 1/2 is?
quiz.mistake: Averages with the wrong pair

quiz.q: Ananya says: 'Between any two different rationals there is at least one more rational.' Is she right?
options: Only for fractions with the same denominator
Yes, their average is always between them
quiz.explain: For a < b, (a + b)/2 is rational and lies between a and b.
steps: For rationals a < b, (a + b)/2 is rational.
It lies between a and b.
So there is always at least one more rational between them.
Answer: Yes, their average is always between them
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'next fraction' exists as for integers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Is there any fraction between 1/3 and 1/2? How many?"
teach.praise: Fantastic! Use averages or bigger denominators, and you'll find infinitely many!
teach.nudge: How can you build one in between? How many do you think there are?

revise.summary: Rational numbers are dense: between any two there are infinitely many more. Use averages, bigger common denominators or extra decimal places to find them.
focus: Find a given number of rationals between two rationals.
Use the average method.
Use decimals to find rationals between.
traps: There is no 'next' rational as there is for integers.
Don't add tops and bottoms to find a fraction between.
Don't include the end points.

learn.hook: Mummy has 13½ metres of cloth. How many kurtas of 2¼ metres can the tailor cut?
points: Turn mixed numbers into improper fractions first: 2¼ = 9/4 and 13½ = 27/2.
'How many pieces of size b fit in a?' means a ÷ b. Any leftover is a − (number of pieces × b).
To solve an equation with fractions, multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators to clear them, then solve as usual.
Always check by putting the answer back into the original equation or story.

example.q: How many kurtas need 2¼ m each from 13½ m of cloth?

learn.reallife: Dividing a 2½ kg box of sweets into ¼ kg packets for Diwali gifts is exactly this kind of problem.

games.title: Solve x/3 + x/4 = 14
items: Multiply by 12: 4x + 3x = 168

quiz.q: A 15 m roll of ribbon is cut into pieces of 1¼ m. How many pieces?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 1¼ instead of dividing

quiz.q: A tailor has 10 m of cloth. Each shirt needs 2⅓ m. How many complete shirts can she make?
quiz.explain: 10 ÷ 7/3 = 30/7 ≈ 4.29, so only 4 complete shirts.
quiz.mistake: Rounds up or gives a fraction of a shirt

quiz.q: For the same 10 m and 2⅓ m shirts, how much cloth is left after 4 shirts?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts one shirt length only
Subtracts 3 from only the numerator

quiz.explain: Cross-multiply: 4(2x − 1) = 3(x + 2), so 8x − 4 = 3x + 6.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only one side by the LCM

quiz.q: Kiran spends 1/4 of her pocket money on books and 1/3 on snacks and has ₹150 left. How much pocket money did she have?
quiz.mistake: Takes 1/4 + 1/3 as the remaining fraction

quiz.q: A recipe for 4 needs 2½ cups of rice. How many cups for 10 people?
quiz.explain: Rice per person = (5/2)/4 = 5/8 cup; for 10: 50/8 = 25/4 = 6¼.
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 instead of scaling

quiz.q: Solve 3x/5 − 2 = x/5.
quiz.explain: Multiply by 5: 3x − 10 = x, so 2x = 10.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply the 2 by 5

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I solve an equation full of fractions?"
teach.praise: Great! Multiply by the LCM to clear fractions, solve, then check!
teach.nudge: What can you multiply both sides by to get rid of the denominators?

revise.summary: For fraction problems, change mixed numbers to improper fractions, divide to find how many pieces fit, and clear fractions in equations by multiplying by the LCM.
focus: Solve 'how many pieces' problems by division.
Find leftovers.
Solve equations with fractions.
traps: Divide by the piece size; don't multiply.
Multiply every term by the LCM, on both sides.
Scale a recipe by the ratio, don't just add.

learn.hook: The diagonal of a 1 m square tile cannot be written as any fraction at all. Here's the proof!
points: The diagonal of a unit square has length √2 (by Pythagoras, 1² + 1² = 2). No fraction p/q has square exactly 2.
Proof by contradiction (linked to Hippasus): suppose √2 = p/q in lowest form. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k.
Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², so q is even too. Both even contradicts 'lowest form', so √2 is irrational.
The same idea works for √3, √5 and √p for any prime p: if p divides a², then p divides a.
For √5: assume √5 = a/b in lowest terms; a² = 5b², so 5 divides a; write a = 5c; then 25c² = 5b², b² = 5c², so 5 divides b. Contradiction.

example.q: In the proof that √3 is irrational, why does a² = 3b² mean 3 divides a?
steps: If a prime divides a square, it divides the number itself
example.answer: Because 3 is prime, 3 | a² gives 3 | a

learn.reallife: Tile-setters cutting a square tile diagonally use √2 ≈ 1.414 times the side, knowing the exact value never ends.

games.title: Proof that √2 is irrational
items: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest form
Square: p² = 2q², so p is even
Write p = 2k, so q² = 2k²
So q is even too
Contradiction: p/q was not in lowest form

games.title: Proof check
items: If p² is even then p is even.
An odd number squared is odd, so p cannot be odd.
The proof assumes p/q is in lowest form.
The contradiction is that both turn out even.
The same proof shows √4 is irrational.
√4 = 2; the step 'if 4 divides a² then 4 divides a' fails (a = 2).
If 5 divides a², then 5 divides a.
5 is prime.
The diagonal of a unit square is 2.
It is √2.

quiz.q: What is the length of the diagonal of a square of side 1 m?
quiz.explain: By Pythagoras, d² = 1² + 1² = 2.
steps: Diagonal d of a 1 m square: d² = 1² + 1² = 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of using Pythagoras

quiz.q: A proof by contradiction starts by:
options: assuming what you want to prove
assuming the opposite of what you want to prove
quiz.explain: You assume √2 is rational and show that this leads to something impossible.
steps: Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite.
To prove √2 irrational, assume √2 is rational.
Then show this leads to something impossible.
Answer: assuming the opposite of what you want to prove
quiz.mistake: Thinks a proof checks examples

quiz.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational, from p² = 2q² we conclude:
quiz.explain: p² is twice a whole number, so it is even; only even numbers have even squares.
steps: p² = 2q² is twice a whole number, so p² is even.
Only even numbers have even squares.
quiz.mistake: Concludes about q before p

quiz.q: After writing p = 2k, the equation p² = 2q² becomes:
quiz.explain: (2k)² = 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the 2 in 2k

quiz.q: What is the contradiction at the end of the √2 proof?
options: p and q are both even, but p/q was in lowest form
quiz.explain: Lowest form means no common factor, yet both share the factor 2.
steps: p/q was chosen in lowest form: no common factor.
The proof shows p and q are both even.
Both sharing factor 2 contradicts lowest form.
Answer: p and q are both even, but p/q was in lowest form
quiz.mistake: Does not see why both being even is a problem

quiz.q: For √5 = a/b in lowest form, a² = 5b². Writing a = 5c gives:
quiz.explain: 25c² = 5b², so b² = 5c², which means 5 divides b as well.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 25 instead of 5

quiz.q: Which key fact makes the √p proof work for a prime p?
options: Every number has a square root
If p divides a², then p divides a
quiz.explain: For primes this is true; it is what forces both a and b to share the factor p.
steps: The key step: if prime p divides a², then p divides a.
This forces both a and b to share the factor p.
Answer: If p divides a², then p divides a
quiz.mistake: Thinks the proof works for any number, prime or not

quiz.q: Why does the same argument NOT prove √9 is irrational?
options: Because the proof only works for 2
quiz.explain: 9 divides a² does not force 9 to divide a (e.g. a = 3). And indeed √9 = 3 is rational.
steps: 9 is a perfect square: √9 = 3, which is rational.
Also 9 is not prime: 9 | a² does not force 9 | a (try a = 3).
Answer: Because 9 is a perfect square: √9 = 3
quiz.mistake: Applies the proof blindly to every square root

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can anyone prove √2 is not a fraction?"
teach.praise: Amazing! Assume it's a fraction in lowest form, show both parts are even, contradiction!
teach.nudge: How does the proof begin? What goes wrong with p and q?

revise.summary: √2 is irrational: assuming √2 = p/q in lowest form forces p and q to both be even, a contradiction. The same proof works for √p when p is prime.
focus: Write the proof that √2 is irrational.
Adapt it for √3 or √5.
Know why it fails for perfect squares.
remember: p² = 2q² → p even → p = 2k → q² = 2k² → q even: contradiction.
Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
traps: Conclude about p before q.
(2k)² = 4k², not 2k².
The proof does not apply to √9 = 3.

learn.hook: √2 is not a fraction, yet you can mark it exactly on a number line with just a ruler and a compass. Here is the trick!
points: Rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers.
Every real number is a point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number. The line has no gaps.
To mark √2: draw a right triangle on the line with legs 1 and 1. Its hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2; swing an arc from 0 with that length.
In the same way, legs 2 and 1 give √5, and legs √2 and 1 give √3.
To compare roots, compare squares: √10 < 3.2 because 10 < 3.2² = 10.24.

example.q: Show how to mark √5 on the number line.
steps: Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line
At A, draw AB = 1 unit perpendicular to the line
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the line at P. Then OP = √5 ≈ 2.24
example.answer: P is the point √5, a little to the right of 2.2

learn.reallife: A ruler with marks only at whole and half centimetres still contains the point √2 cm: every length you can draw is a real number.

quiz.q: Between which two whole numbers does √20 lie?
quiz.explain: 4² = 16 and 5² = 25. Since 16 < 20 < 25, √20 lies between 4 and 5.
quiz.mistake: Looks at numbers near 20 instead of the squares near 20

quiz.q: To mark √2 on the number line, which right triangle do you draw?
quiz.explain: With legs 1 and 1 the hypotenuse is √(1² + 1²) = √2.
quiz.mistake: Uses legs 1 and 2, which give √5 instead

quiz.q: Which is greater, √10 or 3.2?
quiz.explain: Compare squares: (√10)² = 10 and 3.2² = 10.24. Since 10 < 10.24, 3.2 is greater.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number with a root sign must be bigger, or guesses √10 ≈ 3.3

quiz.q: From 0 on a number line, Arjun marks 3 units, draws a 2-unit perpendicular there and swings the hypotenuse down onto the line. Which number does he get?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is √(3² + 2²) = √(9 + 4) = √13.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs (5) or forgets to take the square root (13)

quiz.q: Which statement about the number line is true?
options: Only rational numbers can be marked on it
√2 cannot be shown on it because its decimals never end
Every point on it stands for a real number
There are gaps that no number fills
quiz.explain: The real numbers fill the whole line: each point is a real number and each real number has a point.
steps: Rationals and irrationals together are the real numbers.
Every point on the line is a real number, and the line has no gaps.
√2 can be marked using a right triangle.
Answer: Every point on it stands for a real number
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number must have a finite decimal to have a place on the line

quiz.q: Which list is in increasing order?
quiz.mistake: Thinks √2 is bigger than 1.5

quiz.q: Riya jumps √9 units and then √16 more units to the right of 0. Where does she land?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, so she lands at 3 + 4 = 7. Note that √9 + √16 is not the same as √(9 + 16) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Writes √9 + √16 = √25 = 5, adding under one root

quiz.q: √50 is closest to which value?
quiz.explain: 7² = 49, so √50 is just a little more than 7. In fact 7.07² ≈ 49.98.
quiz.mistake: Halves the number instead of taking its square root

teach.ask: Gappu holds a compass: "How can I put √2 on a number line if I can't even write it as a fraction?"
teach.praise: A right triangle with sides 1 and 1, then swing the hypotenuse down with a compass. √2 has a home on the line!
teach.nudge: What shape do I draw first, and how do I bring its long side down onto the line?

revise.summary: Rationals and irrationals together form the real numbers, which fill the number line with no gaps. √2, √3 and √5 can be marked using right triangles.
focus: Mark √2, √3 and √5 on the number line.
Compare roots by comparing squares.
Know that every point is a real number.
remember: Legs 1 and 1 → √2; legs 2 and 1 → √5; legs √2 and 1 → √3.
traps: Legs 1 and 2 give √5, not √2.
A number does not need a finite decimal to have a place on the line.

topics.title: The square-root spiral, π and the journey of numbers

learn.hook: A spiral of right triangles draws √2, √3, √4, √5 ... one after another like a snail shell!
points: Square-root spiral: start with a right triangle with legs 1 and 1 (hypotenuse √2). On that hypotenuse put a new leg of 1 at right angles: the new hypotenuse is √3, then √4 = 2, √5, and so on.
π, the ratio of circumference to diameter, is irrational. Aryabhata gave the approximation 62832/20000 = 3927/1250 = 3.1416.
Madhava of Sangamagrama found the infinite series π = 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + ...).
Number systems grew by need: N (counting) → Z (debts, zero) → Q (sharing) → irrationals (lengths like √2) → R (the whole number line).
A teaser: no real number squared is negative, so mathematicians later invented i = √(−1), the start of complex numbers.

example.q: In the square-root spiral, what is the hypotenuse of the 7th triangle?

learn.reallife: Space agencies use π to many decimal places for orbits, but Aryabhata's 3.1416 is already accurate to 4 decimal places.

games.title: How number systems grew
items: Natural numbers N
Integers Z
Rational numbers Q
Irrational numbers
Real numbers R

quiz.q: In the square-root spiral, the hypotenuse after √5 is:
quiz.explain: Each new triangle adds a leg of 1: (√5)² + 1² = 6.
steps: Each new triangle adds a leg of 1 to the last hypotenuse.
quiz.mistake: Squares the previous hypotenuse length incorrectly

quiz.q: Which hypotenuse in the spiral is a whole number?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3. (√4 = 2 and √16 = 4 are the others.)
steps: √n is whole only when n is a perfect square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks no hypotenuse can be whole

quiz.q: Aryabhata's value of π is 3927/1250. What is it as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 3927 ÷ 1250 = 3.1416, and π = 3.14159... so this is correct to four decimal places.
steps: Answer: 3.1416, correct to four decimal places
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 22/7 ≈ 3.1428

quiz.q: What are the first three terms inside Madhava's series for π?
quiz.explain: The series uses odd denominators with alternating signs, all multiplied by 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses all whole numbers instead of odd numbers

quiz.q: Using just the first three terms, 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5) = ?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by 4

quiz.q: Is π rational or irrational?
quiz.explain: π's decimals never end and never repeat; 22/7 = 3.142857... is close but not equal.
steps: π's decimals never end and never repeat, so π is irrational.
Answer: Irrational; 22/7 is only an approximation
quiz.mistake: Thinks 22/7 is the exact value of π

quiz.q: Which number system was needed to answer 'what is 3 − 5?'
quiz.explain: 3 − 5 = −2 needs negative numbers, which the integers include.
steps: Natural numbers have no negatives; integers do.
quiz.mistake: Thinks natural numbers include negatives

quiz.q: Why is i = √(−1) not a real number?
options: Because square roots are always irrational
No real number squared gives a negative number
quiz.explain: Every real number squared is 0 or positive, so √(−1) needs a new kind of number.
steps: Any real number squared is 0 or positive.
So no real number has square −1.
√(−1) needs a new kind of number, i.
Answer: No real number squared gives a negative number
quiz.mistake: Thinks √(−1) = −1

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How did we go from counting numbers to real numbers?"
teach.praise: Beautiful! Counting, then negatives, fractions, irrationals, and finally all reals!
teach.nudge: What came after natural numbers? What kind of number is √2?

revise.summary: The square-root spiral builds √2, √3, √4, ... by adding legs of 1. π is irrational; Aryabhata gave 3.1416 and Madhava an infinite series. Number systems grew by need, from N to R.
focus: Find hypotenuses in the square-root spiral.
Know Aryabhata's and Madhava's work on π.
Trace N → Z → Q → R and why i is not real.
remember: No real number squared is negative, so i = √(−1) is not real.
traps: 22/7 is not the exact value of π.
Madhava's series uses odd denominators, not all whole numbers.

learn.hook: Divide 1 by 8 and the division stops. Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 go round and round forever. Why?
points: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates (ends), like 3/8 = 0.375, or is non-terminating and recurring (repeats), like 1/3 = 0.333...
A fraction in lowest terms terminates only if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/20 terminates, but 5/12 repeats.
An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring: it never ends and never settles into a repeating block.
A repeating decimal can be turned back into p/q. For 0.777..., let x = 0.777...; then 10x = 7.777..., so 9x = 7 and x = 7/9.
The repeating block is shown with a bar on top, for example 0.27 with a bar on 27 means 0.272727...

example.q: Write 0.474747... (47 repeating) in the form p/q.
steps: Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 47.474747...

learn.reallife: When ₹100 is shared equally among 3 friends, each share is ₹33.333..., so in real life we round it to ₹33.33.

games.title: What kind of decimal?
items: π

items.q: 0.454545... (45 repeating) as a fraction in lowest terms

quiz.q: What is the decimal expansion of 7/8?
quiz.explain: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. The division ends because 8 = 2³ has only the prime factor 2.
quiz.mistake: Just writes the numerator and denominator side by side after the point

quiz.q: Which fraction has a terminating decimal expansion?
quiz.explain: 40 = 2³ × 5 has only 2s and 5s, so 11/40 = 0.275 terminates. 7, 12 = 2² × 3 and 9 = 3² all contain other primes.
steps: Terminates only if the denominator (lowest form) has primes 2 and 5 only.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an even denominator always gives a terminating decimal

quiz.q: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is:
quiz.explain: If the decimal ended or repeated, the number could be written as p/q and would be rational.
steps: If an irrational's decimal ended or repeated, it could be written as p/q.
So its decimal never ends and never repeats.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any decimal that goes on forever is irrational, even if it repeats

quiz.q: Write 0.777... (7 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.explain: Let x = 0.777...; 10x = 7.777...; subtracting gives 9x = 7, so x = 7/9.
quiz.mistake: Writes 7/10, treating the repeating decimal as if it stopped after one digit

quiz.q: Write 0.363636... (36 repeating) in lowest terms.
quiz.explain: Two digits repeat: 100x − x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11.
quiz.mistake: Uses 90 instead of 99 when two digits repeat

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857142857... How many digits are in its repeating block?
quiz.explain: The block 142857 repeats, and it has 6 digits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the block length must equal the denominator 7

quiz.q: Aisha shares ₹100 equally among 3 friends. Which describes 100/3 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.333..., with 3 repeating forever. It repeats, so it is rational, not irrational.
steps: 100 ÷ 3 = 33 remainder 1, and each further step gives 3 again.
A repeating decimal is rational, not irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rounded money value is the exact answer

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.explain: In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing, so no fixed block repeats. It never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.
steps: 0.1212... repeats, 0.125 terminates, 12/99 is a fraction: all rational.
In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing.
No block repeats and it never ends, so it is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long decimal is irrational without checking for a repeating block

teach.ask: Gappu taps the calculator: "Some decimals stop, some repeat and some go wild. How can I tell which numbers are rational from their decimals?"
teach.praise: Decimals that end or repeat belong to rational numbers; decimals that never end and never repeat are irrational. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: What happens to the decimal of 1/3 compared with √2? Does one of them repeat?

revise.summary: A rational number's decimal either terminates or repeats; an irrational's never ends and never repeats. A fraction in lowest form terminates only if its denominator has only 2s and 5s.
focus: Decide if a fraction terminates or repeats.
Convert repeating decimals to p/q.
Identify irrational decimals.
traps: An even denominator does not guarantee termination: 5/12 repeats.
A decimal that goes on forever but repeats is rational.
Use 99 when two digits repeat, not 90.

topics.title: Decimals to fractions and cyclic numbers

learn.hook: 1/7 hides a magic number: 142857. Multiply it by 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 and the same digits just rotate!
points: If p/q in lowest form has q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, the decimal ends after the larger of m and n places: 7/40 = 7/(2³ × 5) has 3 places (0.175).
Terminating decimal to fraction: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8.
Repeating decimal: if x = 0.4545..., 100x = 45.4545..., so 99x = 45 and x = 5/11. For a mixed repeating decimal like 0.1666..., use 10x = 1.666... and 100x = 16.666...; then 90x = 15, x = 1/6.
0.999... = 1: if x = 0.999..., then 10x = 9.999..., so 9x = 9 and x = 1. Some numbers have two decimal forms.
1/7 = 0.142857..., and 2/7, 3/7, ..., 6/7 use the same six digits rotated (2/7 = 0.285714...). The fractions k/13 split into two such rotating families: 076923 and 153846.
learn.reallife: Bank interest rates like 7.5% per year are terminating decimals because their denominators are made of 2s and 5s.

quiz.q: How many decimal places does 13/80 have?
quiz.explain: 80 = 2⁴ × 5. The larger power is 4, so 4 places: 13/80 = 0.1625.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of digits in the denominator

quiz.q: Write 0.64 as a fraction in lowest form.
quiz.mistake: Reduces only part way

quiz.q: Write 0.272727... (27 repeating) as a fraction in lowest form.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 as the denominator, as for a terminating decimal

quiz.q: Write 0.8333... (3 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as a pure repeating decimal

quiz.q: Using x = 0.999..., what does 10x − x give?
quiz.explain: 10x = 9.999..., and subtracting x removes all the 9s after the point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 0.999... must be less than 1

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857... What is 3/7 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 3/7 uses the same digits rotated, starting from 4: 0.428571...
steps: k/7 uses the six digits of 142857 rotated.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3/7 is 3 times each digit separately

quiz.q: What is 142857 × 7?
quiz.mistake: Expects the answer to be a rotation of 142857

quiz.q: 1/13 = 0.076923... Which of these is a rotation of 076923 and so belongs to the same family?
quiz.explain: 769230 is 076923 rotated. 2/13, 5/13 and 7/13 belong to the other family, 153846.
steps: 153846, 384615 and 538461 belong to the other family.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every k/13 uses the same six digits

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I turn 0.444... into a fraction?"
teach.praise: Super! Let x be the decimal, multiply by 10, subtract, and solve: 4/9!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply x by? What do you do with the two equations?

revise.summary: If q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, p/q ends after the larger of m and n places. Repeating decimals convert to fractions by multiplying and subtracting; 0.999... = 1; sevenths and thirteenths form cyclic families.
focus: Convert terminating and repeating decimals to fractions.
Handle mixed repeating decimals.
Use cyclic patterns of 1/7 and 1/13.
traps: 0.999... is not less than 1.
A mixed repeating decimal needs 10x and 100x, not just 100x.
Not every k/13 uses the same six digits.
